title: Deep Learning Recommenders
summary: Modern neural recommenders that scale collaborative filtering past matrix factorization's limits, up to hundreds of millions of items.

slides.markdown:
Matrix factorization scores a user-item pair with a fixed dot product — a fundamentally linear interaction. **Neural collaborative filtering (NCF)** replaces that dot product with a learned function: concatenate (or otherwise combine) the user and item embeddings and feed them through a small multi-layer perceptron to produce the score.

The payoff is expressiveness — an MLP can learn non-linear interactions a dot product structurally cannot (e.g. "this user loves this item only when it's *both* recent and in their favorite genre," which is an AND of features, not a weighted sum). The cost is more parameters and slower inference than a plain dot product.

A **two-tower model** has two independent neural networks — a **user tower** that embeds a user (and their context) into a vector, and an **item tower** that embeds an item into a vector in the same space. The score is the dot product (or cosine similarity) of the two output embeddings.

The key architectural choice is keeping the towers separate rather than combining features early like NCF does — because it means item embeddings can be **precomputed offline** for the entire catalog, and user embeddings computed once per request, so scoring becomes a nearest-neighbor lookup instead of a forward pass per candidate.

slides.subTitle: Why they scale to huge catalogs
slides.markdown:
This precomputation is what unlocks scale to hundreds of millions of items. At serving time, you don't run a neural net over every candidate item — you embed the user *once*, then use **approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search** (e.g. FAISS, ScaNN) over the precomputed item embedding index to retrieve the top candidates in milliseconds.

This is why two-tower models are the standard **candidate generation** stage in industry recommenders (YouTube, Instagram) — they're built specifically to make retrieval over a massive catalog cheap, leaving the more expensive, feature-rich ranking model for a much smaller shortlist.

Static user embeddings miss something obvious: **what you want next often depends on what you just did**, not just your long-run taste. Sequence-aware recommenders (built on RNNs, or more often Transformers today, see [rnn-lstm-sequence-models](rnn-lstm-sequence-models)) model a user's session or recent history as an ordered sequence and predict the next likely interaction.

This is why buying a phone case right after buying a phone gets recommended immediately, and why a music session that just went acoustic keeps recommending acoustic — the model conditions on *recency and order*, not a static average of all-time preferences.

| | Matrix factorization | Two-tower neural model |
|---|---|---|
| Input features | User/item ID only | IDs plus rich features (text, images, context, recency) |
| Scoring at serving time | Dot product lookup | Dot product over precomputed embeddings + ANN search |
| Handles new items/users | Poorly (needs the ID to already exist) | Better (features generalize to unseen IDs) |
| Scale to huge catalogs | Good | Excellent — purpose-built for it |

**How to decide:** reach for two-tower when you have rich side features and a catalog too large to score exhaustively; plain matrix factorization is still a fine, cheap baseline when your only signal is the interaction matrix itself.

It's tempting to think deep collaborative models finally "solve" cold start because they're more powerful. They don't — a purely collaborative signal (ID embeddings learned from interactions) still has nothing to say about a user or item with zero history, no matter how deep the network is.

What actually helps is feeding in **content features** (item text/image embeddings, user demographics) alongside the ID embeddings, so the model has *something* to fall back on when the ID embedding is untrained. That's a hybrid design decision, not a side effect of using a neural net.
